name: Script Signals & Payoff
oneLine: Script signals are the bodily tells - a sigh, a tensed sphincter, a stomach drop - that someone has just moved into script. The payoff is the closing scene the whole script was always organized to arrive at.
whatYouDid: You caught Imran's stomach-drop at the knock on his door as the script signal it was, then chose a response sized to the actual typo instead of to the old threat his body still expected.

fromBook.quote: Eric Berne wrote of script signals. These are bodily clues that indicate a person has moved into script... Berne drew attention especially to tensions in the sphincters, the muscles that close the various body openings.

expand.definition: The payoff is written into the script from the start, as Berne's own definition insists ('culminating in a chosen alternative') - each scripty moment, including the small ones a script signal announces, is unawarely organized to move a step closer to that final scene.
expand.otherFraming: Berne's own, more colloquial name for carrying a payoff around as a readable, repeating identity is the 'sweatshirt' metaphor - a phrase from outside this project's four core books, but one most TA writers use for exactly this idea.
expand.tryThisToday: Notice your own script signal once today - the specific bodily tell, not just 'feeling off' - and use it as information that you've just stepped into an old scene, not as the scene's instructions.
